title: Pass the Passkey: A Novel Attack Surface in Passwordless Authentication
excerpt: Explore how passkey implementation gaps undermine security when relying parties fail to validate the User Verified flag, reducing MFA to a single factor.
content_html:
Executive Summary

This article analyzes new attack classes against passwordless authentication, focusing on Google’s synced passkey ecosystem and the Cloud Authenticator used by desktop clients. The attacks demonstrate how malware on a compromised endpoint can misuse onboarding, recovery and device trust workflows to take over passkey-protected accounts. We show how an attacker can authenticate without user interaction, bypass user verification requirements and extract all synced passkey private keys.

After decades of breaches and billions in losses, the attack vectors that defined the era of passwords and shared secrets are finally starting to fade. Passkeys replace passwords and traditional multi-factor authentication (MFA) with public-key cryptography, decreasing entire classes of attacks that have dominated the threat landscape for years.

With no shared secret to steal, reuse or phish, many of an attacker’s most reliable tools are becoming obsolete. This represents a significant disruption for the credential theft market.

Attackers, however, persist. They evolve, and defenders must prepare for a new generation of attacks. As passkeys become widely adopted and scale to billions of accounts, defenders must prepare for new attack surfaces, some of which we disclose in our research.

This article is part 3 in our series examining passkey adoption from a security perspective. If you haven’t read the previous parts, we recommend starting here:

Part 1: The Art of the Invisible Key – Passkey Global Breakthrough

Part 2: Google Authenticator: The Hidden Mechanisms of Passwordless Authentication

Setting the Stage

Google’s synced passkey implementation is particularly instructive due to its scale and how it creates a higher standard for private key protection in two critical ways:

  • Private keys are generated and used within a cloud-enclave isolation environment
  • Hardware-backed, client-device-bound keys control access to cloud-based cryptographic operations, attesting to the user’s presence on a trusted device

This article builds on the architectural analysis from Part 1 and Part 2 of our previous articles in this series. We now shift from how passkeys are built and deployed to how attackers can misuse them.

We present three novel attacks that enable account takeover of passkey-protected accounts. Each attack challenges a different core assumption of passkey authentication security. When a client authenticates with a passkey, the following is expected:

  • Users provide explicit consent on the device to verify user presence
  • For MFA, users must also unlock the device to verify biometric (i.e., something you are) or knowledge-based (i.e., something you know) authentication factors
  • Passkey private keys cannot be shared or copied

The Google documentation reflects these core assumptions, describing the passkey login process as a secure alternative to passwords (as shown in Figure 1).

Challenging these expectations is a category of attacks we've nicknamed Pass-ta-key. This playful, layered name blends the word passkey and the phrase “pass the key,” with a light nod to the concept of plate of pasta, illustrating how tangled this key implementation can get.

These attacks each expose a different weakness in practice:

  • Pass-ta-key attack: An attacker takes over an account protected by a Google-synced passkey using malware running on the victim’s device, without requiring privilege escalation, device unlock or user interaction
  • Silver Pass-ta-key attack: An attacker deceives the Google Cloud Authenticator into believing the victim has unlocked the device with biometrics, leading to full account takeover without using the victim’s device during authentication
  • Golden Pass-ta-key attack: An attacker can extract all synced passkeys in a form that allows them to be shared or sold on the credential black market

These attacks demonstrate how malware can exploit synced passkeys, even when providers add hardware-backed protections to secure credentials within the cloud authenticator.

Disclaimer: This research involved responsible and ethical security analysis. We responsibly disclosed all presented exploits. The cloud authenticator model is used by various passkey providers across multiple browsers and platforms. This work, however, focuses on Google Password Manager in Chrome on Windows, specifically on devices equipped with a Trusted Platform Module (TPM). All presented attacks rely on malware already existing on the victim’s device during the initial stage.

Stage Zero Reconnaissance

Before attempting any of the attacks, the attacker needs visibility into how passkeys are used within the victim’s account. On a compromised endpoint, this visibility is readily available.

Chrome locally stores synced passkey data as part of its synchronization process. On Windows, Chrome persists this data as proto-encoded WebauthnCredentialSpecifics records, which represent synced WebAuthn credentials, within its sync database:

%LocalAppData%\Google\Chrome\User Data\<Profile>\Sync Data\LevelDB

Accessing these records does not require elevated privileges. The records allow an attacker to enumerate where the victim uses passkeys, along with associated usernames, credential identifiers and the encrypted private key.

After identifying a service where the victim uses passkeys, an attacker can attempt to authenticate as the victim.

The primary challenge for attackers is bypassing the protection of the private key, which is used to sign authentication challenges. This private key is secured by a master key. While an encrypted version of this master key is stored on each client device, only the cloud authenticator can decrypt it.

Despite this security, the architecture remains vulnerable to exploitation. The following sections detail methods attackers could use to exploit system mechanisms, authenticate as the victim, and compromise passkey-secured accounts.

Device Identity Impersonation: The Pass-Ta-Key Attack

Our first attack is the most straightforward approach, which involves taking over a passkey-protected account by mimicking the behavior of Google Password Manager and Chrome during legitimate authentication. In a normal flow, Chrome sends a request to the cloud authenticator, signed using the device’s hardware-backed keys.

Unlike a legitimate user flow that requires user interaction and device unlock, this attack shows how malware can obtain the required signature silently, without user consent, biometrics, device unlock or elevated privileges.

To understand this, we focus on Chrome’s device identity key, which represents client device possession to the cloud authenticator. As previously explained (part 2: Login with Synced Passkey and Device Key Signature), generating the required assertion involves signing data sent to the cloud authenticator using one of the device’s hardware-backed keys. This is the identity key or the user verification key (UV key).

Although both keys are hardware-bound, they are not accessed in the same way. For the identity key, Chrome creates the conditions that allow it to request a signature while running as a user without elevated privileges and without triggering device unlock protections.

On Windows, Chrome calls the NcryptCreatePersistedKey function without assigning a key name, making the TPM-backed key ephemeral and preventing it from being persisted to disk. Instead of storing the private key within the TPM, Chrome calls NcryptExportKey to export the key as an NCRYPT_OPAQUE_KEY_BLOB, which instructs the TPM to encrypt the private key using a TPM-resident key. The resulting blob is stored as wrapped_identity_private_key in the passkey_enclave_state file, making it available for future use on the same physical TPM.

Malware can extract this wrapped_identity_private_key from disk or Chrome’s memory. It can then invoke cryptographic operations using standard Windows Cryptography API: Next Generation (CNG) APIs (NCryptOpenStorageProvider, NCryptImportKey, NCryptSignHash), without elevated privileges, mimicking Chrome’s own actions.

Having established that malware can generate the required signature, we now detail the full Pass-ta-key attack flow (as shown in Figure 2). This flow allows a remote attacker with unprivileged malware on the victim’s device to authenticate as the victim.

The attack flow consists of the following phases:

  1. After collecting the victim’s synced passkey records (Stage Zero: Reconnaissance), the attacker selects a targeted account and initiates a passkey login
  2. The relying party responds with a fresh authentication challenge
  3. The attacker initiates a WebSocket handshake with the Google Cloud Authenticator
  4. Using the hash of that handshake, the attacker interacts with the victim’s TPM and uses the extracted identity key to sign the handshake hash together with the assertion request
  5. The attacker sends an assertion request to the cloud authenticator, including the identity key signature
  6. From the cloud authenticator’s perspective, the request appears to be a trusted device making a valid request, so it produces a valid assertion response
  7. This assertion is then forwarded to the relying party, completing authentication and giving the attacker full control of the victim’s account

Video 1 demonstrates the attack as it would unfold in practice. (We have blurred the names of the relying parties to avoid naming.)

Video 1. Example of a successful Pass-ta-key attack.

As the video begins, the screen splits between the attacker's terminal and the victim's desktop. The video first shows the attacker establishing a command-and-control (C2) listener, passively waiting for victims to connect.

On the victim’s machine, the Trojan executes as a standard user, without elevated privileges. Once active, it collects the victim’s encrypted, synced passkeys and sends them back to the attacker’s C2 server. This provides visibility into the victim’s available passkeys.

The attacker selects a target, such as a messaging application account protected by a passkey, navigates to the application and chooses Login with passkey. The relying party then responds with a fresh authentication challenge.

Next, the attacker initiates communication with the Google Cloud Authenticator. After completing the handshake, the attacker triggers the Trojan to use the device’s identity key to sign the required data. Specifically, it uses the hash of the handshake combined with the hash of the serialized assertion request.

The attacker then attaches this signature to the request sent to the cloud authenticator. The cloud authenticator returns the requested assertion. The attacker forwards this valid assertion to the relying party and successfully logs in as the victim.

UV Flag: When MFA Depends on a Single Bit

The Pass-ta-key attack is effective when the relying party does not strictly require user verification. Many relying parties configure WebAuthn’s userVerification parameter as preferred rather than required to support diverse devices and user experiences, making them susceptible to this attack.

When a relying party explicitly requires user verification, one would expect the cloud authenticator to reject requests that are not signed using a key gated by PIN or biometric verification. Surprisingly, this is not the case.

The cloud authenticator returns a valid assertion regardless of whether the request was signed using the identity key or the UV key. The difference comes down to a single bit in the authenticator data, the User Verified (UV) flag.

When the assertion is signed using the UV key, this flag is set to 1. When it is signed using the identity key, the flag remains 0.

While the Pass-ta-key attack produces cryptographically valid assertions matching the relying party’s public key, our testing shows attacks typically fail when user verification is required because the UV flag remains unset. For example, when attempting the attack against a passkey-protected GitHub account, the attacker receives an error message, as shown in Figure 3.

Although authentication is typically rejected when user verification is required, this behavior is not always consistently enforced across relying parties. In our testing, we identified relying parties that accepted authentication because they did not properly validate the UV flag. This allowed the attack to succeed despite the absence of user verification.

The lack of validation effectively reduces the authentication process to a single factor. By compromising only the device identity key, the attacker is able to authenticate successfully and take over the account, even though MFA is required.

We reported this issue to the affected relying parties.

Video 2 demonstrates this behavior in practice on eBay. Although eBay sets the userVerification parameter to required, the demo recording shows a successful passkey login using the described technique, without any user interaction or additional authentication factors.

We captured this recording before eBay fixed the issue. Following our report, eBay addressed this verification gap and now properly validates the UV flag.

Video 2. Pass-ta-key attack succeeds despite the absence of user verification, even when the UV is required.

Pending Attacker: The Silver Pass-Ta-Key Attack

When an account is protected by stronger authentication requirements, such as for financial or federal identity systems, the attacker must also bypass user verification. This initially appears to be a significant challenge.

The cloud authenticator requires a message signed with the UV key to set the UV flag. Client interaction controls access to this key, as the OS validates the user via the same mechanism used for device unlock. Without escalating to system privileges or physical access to the victim device, an attacker has no apparent path to obtain such access.

Attackers can bypass this challenge through the following mechanism:

  • Instead of bypassing access to the UV key, the attacker invalidates the existing key registered in the cloud authenticator and registers a newly generated key under their control
  • Once the attacker-controlled key is registered, any message signed with it is accepted by the cloud authenticator as if the user had successfully performed device unlock

Figure 4 demonstrates the attacker-side authentication flow in the Silver Pass-ta-key attack, focusing on the authentication phase after the attacker-controlled UV key is registered.

This approach has important implications. It allows the attacker to fully automate authentication across all the victim’s accounts without human interaction, even where user verification is enforced. Furthermore, the attacker no longer needs live access to the victim’s device during authentication.

Unlike the previous attack, which required active malware on the victim’s device for each authentication, the Silver attack provides reusable access. This allows the attacker to access the victim’s passkey-protected accounts from their own environment, without requiring the victim’s device to be online or active. Ultimately, this enables account takeover across all passkeys associated with the victim without requiring elevated privileges.

Invalidating the Existing User Verification Key

To carry out this attack, the first objective is to invalidate the existing UV key associated with the target device. From the previous attack, we learned how an attacker can use unprivileged malware to sign attacker-controlled requests with the device identity key and send them to the cloud authenticator. The attacker can leverage this capability to issue a device/forget command on behalf of the victim. A simpler option is to directly delete the victim’s passkey_enclave_state file, as there are no built-in protections that prevent its removal.

Regardless of the method, the next time the user attempts to use a passkey, Chrome is forced to re-onboard the device. This occurs either because Chrome no longer has access to the device key or because the cloud authenticator no longer recognizes the device as registered.

Exploiting the Onboarding Flow

On Windows, device onboarding is only completed after the second use of a passkey on the same device. During the first use, Chrome begins onboarding with the cloud authenticator in the background while prompting the user to enter the Google Password Manager (GPM) recovery PIN.

If Chrome were to create the UV key at this point, it would also trigger a Windows Hello prompt, requiring the user to authenticate again using biometrics or a PIN. Since both steps may involve a PIN, presenting them back-to-back in the same flow can be confusing and lead to user errors. To avoid this, Chrome defers the creation of the UV key.

Instead, the device is initially registered in a uv_key_pending state. During this first interaction, the GPM recovery PIN satisfies user verification, and the actual UV key is only created and registered during the next passkey use, when the additional prompt is no longer needed.

After forcing the victim into this re-registration state, the attacker can exploit the uv_key_pending condition. In their own environment, the attacker generates an asymmetric key pair. They then send a device/add_uv_key command to the cloud authenticator, providing the attacker-controlled public key as the UV key.

The cloud authenticator does not validate the attestation of newly registered UV keys to verify whether they originate from secure hardware. As a result, the attacker-controlled key is stored alongside the legitimate device identity key:

From this point on, the attacker can use the forged UV key to request signatures for any passkey associated with the victim and obtain assertions with the UV bit set. This provides access to high-value accounts even when user verification is enforced and validated.

Stealing the Master Key: The Golden Pass-Ta-Key Attack

In this attack, the attacker effectively gains the cloud authenticator’s superpower, the ability to decrypt synced passkeys. This is particularly impactful because it undermines the intended protection mechanism.

The passkey’s private key is protected using a symmetric master key called the security domain secret (SDS). This master key is not directly accessible, it is stored on the device as an encrypted wrapped_secret. Only the cloud authenticator can decrypt this wrapped_secret using its device-specific key (wrapping_key) within its isolated environment, as noted in Figure 5.

Figure 5. Synced passkey decryption inside the cloud authenticator.

This design aims to protect synced passkeys even if the client device is compromised. As Google noted in response to one of our vulnerability reports:

“The (cloud) enclave authenticator’s primary function is to make it difficult to steal passkey private data, which would be an obvious target for malware if it were locally available.”

The security of this model ultimately hinges on the protection of the 32-byte SDS. If an attacker is able to obtain the SDS, they effectively gain the ability to decrypt all synced passkeys for that account. This allows them to authenticate as a fully verified user and take over every service where the victim relies on passkeys.

Leaking the SDS

This secret should never be exposed to the client device, even during device loss or account recovery. However, we unexpectedly found the SDS present in Chrome’s logs during registration with the cloud authenticator, simply by opening chrome://device-log/FIDO, as noted in Figure 6.

In the current Chrome implementation, every device joining or rejoining an account’s security domain retrieves the SDS from the recovery key store, Google’s Trusted Vault service. The cloud authenticator includes a mechanism that allows Chrome to facilitate the recovery flow where the key cannot be decrypted on the client device, however this mechanism is not used. Instead, Chrome recovers the SDS in an accessible form.

One possible explanation is needing to standardize the device join and recovery process across platforms. Unlike desktop environments, Google Password Manager on iOS and Android does not rely on the cloud authenticator and must obtain the master key to decrypt synced passkeys. As a result, Chrome appears to follow the same recovery model, even though the cloud authenticator could enable a more isolated approach.

Although Google removed this secret from Chrome’s logging output following our report, the SDS is still sent to the client and remains accessible in Chrome’s process memory. If the attacker forces the victim to re-register with the cloud authenticator and knows the pattern to look for, they can extract the SDS directly from memory.

The Golden Pass-ta-key attack allows full account takeover through the following steps:

  1. The attacker forces Chrome to trigger a fresh onboarding using the same mechanisms as the Silver Pass-ta-key attack
  2. The attacker monitors the system for the recreation or modification of the passkey_enclave_state
  3. Once the file is recreated/modified, the attacker dumps Chrome’s process memory and extracts the SDS, which is temporarily present in plaintext
  4. The attacker reads the WebauthnCredentialSpecifics records from Chrome’s sync database (Stage Zero: Reconnaissance)
  5. Using the extracted SDS, the attacker decrypts the encrypted fields in each record and recovers the corresponding passkey private keys
  6. The attacker uses the recovered private keys to sign the relying party’s challenge and successfully authenticates as the victim

Figure 7 shows how an attacker would use the SDS to decrypt passkeys and forge a valid authentication response.

Video 3 shows how an attacker uses the stolen SDS to log in to a high-value account (in this case, a crypto exchange).

Video 3. How an attacker uses the stolen SDS to log in to a high-value account.

The Golden Pass-ta-key attack has a significantly broader impact. Beyond the reusable access from the attacker’s environment, the SDS allows the attacker to decrypt all existing passkeys as well as any future passkeys created for the account.

While the Silver attack is mitigated by unregistering or re-enrolling the device, the Golden attack provides strong persistence. Even if a compromise is detected, remediation is limited. In Google’s current implementation, there is no way to rotate or revoke the SDS, meaning all current and future synced passkeys remain protected by the same master key.

Mitigations

Enforce Strict User Verification (UV) Validation

Relying parties should require userVerification = required and validate the UV flag in all authentication responses. Failure to enforce this check can reduce authentication to a single factor. Figure 8 below shows the authenticator data layout.

Validate Device Key Registration and Attestation

Credential managers should verify the origin and attestation of newly registered device keys, including UV and identity keys. Accepting arbitrary keys without validation allows unauthorized key registration and bypass of user verification requirements.

Harden Recovery and Device Re-Registration Flows

Credential manager recovery PIN prompts are typically associated with onboarding or account recovery, not routine passkey authentication. Unexpected or repeated prompts during normal passkey usage may indicate re-triggering of onboarding or recovery, potentially due to phishing attempts or local manipulation of passkey state.

These flows are security-sensitive because recovery operations can re-establish device trust and restore access to synced credentials. In the scenarios from our research, triggering recovery enabled registration of new verification keys or exposure of key material used to decrypt synced passkeys.

Monitoring agents should detect and restrict unnecessary re-triggering of onboarding and recovery flows, especially after deletion or modification of local passkey state files. Additional verification should be required before re-establishing device trust or recovering synced credentials.

Prevent Exposure of Sensitive Key Material on the Client

Sensitive material such as the master key should not be exposed to the client, including through memory or logs. Instead, credential managers should use designs where cryptographic operations are performed on behalf of the client, without transferring the underlying key material to the client environment.

Restrict Access to Local Passkey Data

Access to passkey-related storage, such as Chrome’s sync database and local state files (e.g., passkey_enclave_state), should be limited to the browser process and protected through platform access controls. This reduces the ability to enumerate credentials, manipulate onboarding state or access device-bound key material from a compromised endpoint.

Improve Detection of Abnormal Passkey Usage

WebAuthn defines a signature counter (signCount) mechanism intended to help relying parties detect cloned or unexpectedly reused credentials. In traditional authenticators, the counter increases with each authentication operation and can provide a signal of abnormal credential usage.

In synchronized passkey systems, authentication assertions commonly contain a constant signCount value. As a result, relying parties and credential providers have limited visibility into unauthorized use of synced credentials, including scenarios where passkeys are extracted or reused from unexpected environments.

Google noted that globally consistent signature counters are difficult to implement in synchronized passkey systems that operate across multiple devices and platforms, particularly when assertions originate from independent clients.

Credential managers that centrally coordinate authentication operations should consider implementing coordinated signature counter mechanisms that account for synchronization and multi-device consistency challenges. Such mechanisms can improve visibility and detection of unexpected credential usage or passkey reuse across environments.

Conclusion

Passkeys represent a meaningful step forward in authentication security. By eliminating shared secrets, they reduce entire classes of attacks that have historically led to widespread account compromise. This changes the economics of credential theft and forces attackers to adopt new techniques.

The attacks presented in this research do not break the underlying cryptography. Instead, they exploit gaps between design assumptions and real-world implementations. These gaps include:

  • Trust placed in client devices
  • Inconsistencies in relying party validation
  • Weaknesses in onboarding and recovery flows

When combined with malware on the endpoint, these gaps enable account takeover scenarios that bypass the guarantees passkeys are expected to provide.

A central takeaway is that endpoint compromise remains a critical part of the threat model. When authentication decisions rely on signals from the user’s device, an attacker with access to that device can manipulate those signals in ways that are difficult to detect. Hardware-backed keys, secure enclaves and cloud isolation significantly raise the bar, but they do not fully eliminate this risk.

Passkey deployments should be treated as one layer in a broader security strategy. Relying parties must enforce strict validation, including proper handling of the user verification signal. Platform providers should continue hardening onboarding and recovery flows, and organizations should invest in protections against malware and memory access on endpoints.

As adoption continues to grow, so will attacker interest in this space. Understanding these emerging attack paths is essential to ensuring passwordless authentication delivers its intended security benefits in real-world conditions.

On Windows, Chrome calls the NcryptCreatePersistedKey function without assigning a key name, making the TPM-backed key ephemeral and preventing it from being persisted to disk. Instead of storing the private key within the TPM, Chrome calls NcryptExportKey to export the key as an NCRYPT_OPAQUE_KEY_BLOB, which instructs the TPM to encrypt the private key using a TPM-resident key. The resulting blob is stored as wrapped_identity_private_key in the passkey_enclave_state file, making it available for future use on the same physical TPM. Malware can extract this wrapped_identity_private_key from disk or Chrome’s memory. It can then invoke cryptographic operations using standard Windows Cryptography API: Next Generation (CNG) APIs (NCryptOpenStorageProvider, NCryptImportKey, NCryptSignHash), without elevated privileges, mimicking Chrome’s own actions. Having established that malware can generate the required signature, we now detail the full Pass-ta-key attack flow (as shown in Figure 2). This flow allows a remote attacker with unprivileged malware on the victim’s device to authenticate as the victim. Figure 2. Pass-ta-key attack flow. The attack flow consists of the following phases: After collecting the victim’s synced passkey records (Stage Zero: Reconnaissance), the attacker selects a targeted account and initiates a passkey login The relying party responds with a fresh authentication challenge The attacker initiates a WebSocket handshake with the Google Cloud Authenticator Using the hash of that handshake, the attacker interacts with the victim’s TPM and uses the extracted identity key to sign the handshake hash together with the assertion request The attacker sends an assertion request to the cloud authenticator, including the identity key signature From the cloud authenticator’s perspective, the request appears to be a trusted device making a valid request, so it produces a valid assertion response This assertion is then forwarded to the relying party, completing authentication and giving the attacker full control of the victim’s account Video 1 demonstrates the attack as it would unfold in practice. (We have blurred the names of the relying parties to avoid naming.) Video 1. Example of a successful Pass-ta-key attack. As the video begins, the screen splits between the attacker's terminal and the victim's desktop. The video first shows the attacker establishing a command-and-control (C2) listener, passively waiting for victims to connect. On the victim’s machine, the Trojan executes as a standard user, without elevated privileges. Once active, it collects the victim’s encrypted, synced passkeys and sends them back to the attacker’s C2 server. This provides visibility into the victim’s available passkeys. The attacker selects a target, such as a messaging application account protected by a passkey, navigates to the application and chooses Login with passkey. The relying party then responds with a fresh authentication challenge. Next, the attacker initiates communication with the Google Cloud Authenticator. After completing the handshake, the attacker triggers the Trojan to use the device’s identity key to sign the required data. Specifically, it uses the hash of the handshake combined with the hash of the serialized assertion request. The attacker then attaches this signature to the request sent to the cloud authenticator. The cloud authenticator returns the requested assertion. The attacker forwards this valid assertion to the relying party and successfully logs in as the victim. UV Flag: When MFA Depends on a Single Bit The Pass-ta-key attack is effective when the relying party does not strictly require user verification. Many relying parties configure WebAuthn’s userVerification parameter as preferred rather than required to support diverse devices and user experiences, making them susceptible to this attack. When a relying party explicitly requires user verification, one would expect the cloud authenticator to reject requests that are not signed using a key gated by PIN or biometric verification. Surprisingly, this is not the case. The cloud authenticator returns a valid assertion regardless of whether the request was signed using the identity key or the UV key. The difference comes down to a single bit in the authenticator data, the User Verified (UV) flag. When the assertion is signed using the UV key, this flag is set to 1. When it is signed using the identity key, the flag remains 0. While the Pass-ta-key attack produces cryptographically valid assertions matching the relying party’s public key, our testing shows attacks typically fail when user verification is required because the UV flag remains unset. For example, when attempting the attack against a passkey-protected GitHub account, the attacker receives an error message, as shown in Figure 3. Figure 3. Message from GitHub passkey login failure. Although authentication is typically rejected when user verification is required, this behavior is not always consistently enforced across relying parties. In our testing, we identified relying parties that accepted authentication because they did not properly validate the UV flag. This allowed the attack to succeed despite the absence of user verification. The lack of validation effectively reduces the authentication process to a single factor. By compromising only the device identity key, the attacker is able to authenticate successfully and take over the account, even though MFA is required. We reported this issue to the affected relying parties. Video 2 demonstrates this behavior in practice on eBay. Although eBay sets the userVerification parameter to required, the demo recording shows a successful passkey login using the described technique, without any user interaction or additional authentication factors. We captured this recording before eBay fixed the issue. Following our report, eBay addressed this verification gap and now properly validates the UV flag. Video 2. Pass-ta-key attack succeeds despite the absence of user verification, even when the UV is required. Pending Attacker: The Silver Pass-Ta-Key Attack When an account is protected by stronger authentication requirements, such as for financial or federal identity systems, the attacker must also bypass user verification. This initially appears to be a significant challenge. The cloud authenticator requires a message signed with the UV key to set the UV flag. Client interaction controls access to this key, as the OS validates the user via the same mechanism used for device unlock. Without escalating to system privileges or physical access to the victim device, an attacker has no apparent path to obtain such access. Attackers can bypass this challenge through the following mechanism: Instead of bypassing access to the UV key, the attacker invalidates the existing key registered in the cloud authenticator and registers a newly generated key under their control Once the attacker-controlled key is registered, any message signed with it is accepted by the cloud authenticator as if the user had successfully performed device unlock Figure 4 demonstrates the attacker-side authentication flow in the Silver Pass-ta-key attack, focusing on the authentication phase after the attacker-controlled UV key is registered. Figure 4. Attacker-side authentication flow in the Silver Pass-ta-key attack. This approach has important implications. It allows the attacker to fully automate authentication across all the victim’s accounts without human interaction, even where user verification is enforced. Furthermore, the attacker no longer needs live access to the victim’s device during authentication. Unlike the previous attack, which required active malware on the victim’s device for each authentication, the Silver attack provides reusable access. This allows the attacker to access the victim’s passkey-protected accounts from their own environment, without requiring the victim’s device to be online or active. Ultimately, this enables account takeover across all passkeys associated with the victim without requiring elevated privileges. Invalidating the Existing User Verification Key To carry out this attack, the first objective is to invalidate the existing UV key associated with the target device. From the previous attack, we learned how an attacker can use unprivileged malware to sign attacker-controlled requests with the device identity key and send them to the cloud authenticator. The attacker can leverage this capability to issue a device/forget command on behalf of the victim. A simpler option is to directly delete the victim’s passkey_enclave_state file, as there are no built-in protections that prevent its removal. Regardless of the method, the next time the user attempts to use a passkey, Chrome is forced to re-onboard the device. This occurs either because Chrome no longer has access to the device key or because the cloud authenticator no longer recognizes the device as registered. Exploiting the Onboarding Flow On Windows, device onboarding is only completed after the second use of a passkey on the same device. During the first use, Chrome begins onboarding with the cloud authenticator in the background while prompting the user to enter the Google Password Manager (GPM) recovery PIN. If Chrome were to create the UV key at this point, it would also trigger a Windows Hello prompt, requiring the user to authenticate again using biometrics or a PIN. Since both steps may involve a PIN, presenting them back-to-back in the same flow can be confusing and lead to user errors. To avoid this, Chrome defers the creation of the UV key. Instead, the device is initially registered in a uv_key_pending state. During this first interaction, the GPM recovery PIN satisfies user verification, and the actual UV key is only created and registered during the next passkey use, when the additional prompt is no longer needed. After forcing the victim into this re-registration state, the attacker can exploit the uv_key_pending condition. In their own environment, the attacker generates an asymmetric key pair. They then send a device/add_uv_key command to the cloud authenticator, providing the attacker-controlled public key as the UV key. The cloud authenticator does not validate the attestation of newly registered UV keys to verify whether they originate from secure hardware. As a result, the attacker-controlled key is stored alongside the legitimate device identity key: 12345 devices[device_id] = { hw: identity_public_key, uv: (Attacker-controlled) uv_public_key } From this point on, the attacker can use the forged UV key to request signatures for any passkey associated with the victim and obtain assertions with the UV bit set. This provides access to high-value accounts even when user verification is enforced and validated. Stealing the Master Key: The Golden Pass-Ta-Key Attack In this attack, the attacker effectively gains the cloud authenticator’s superpower, the ability to decrypt synced passkeys. This is particularly impactful because it undermines the intended protection mechanism. The passkey’s private key is protected using a symmetric master key called the security domain secret (SDS). This master key is not directly accessible, it is stored on the device as an encrypted wrapped_secret. Only the cloud authenticator can decrypt this wrapped_secret using its device-specific key (wrapping_key) within its isolated environment, as noted in Figure 5. Figure 5. Synced passkey decryption inside the cloud authenticator. Figure 5. Synced passkey decryption inside the cloud authenticator. This design aims to protect synced passkeys even if the client device is compromised. As Google noted in response to one of our vulnerability reports: “The (cloud) enclave authenticator’s primary function is to make it difficult to steal passkey private data, which would be an obvious target for malware if it were locally available.” The security of this model ultimately hinges on the protection of the 32-byte SDS. If an attacker is able to obtain the SDS, they effectively gain the ability to decrypt all synced passkeys for that account. This allows them to authenticate as a fully verified user and take over every service where the victim relies on passkeys. Leaking the SDS This secret should never be exposed to the client device, even during device loss or account recovery. However, we unexpectedly found the SDS present in Chrome’s logs during registration with the cloud authenticator, simply by opening chrome://device-log/FIDO, as noted in Figure 6. Figure 6. The SDS (the passkey master key) is exposed in plaintext in the device log. In the current Chrome implementation, every device joining or rejoining an account’s security domain retrieves the SDS from the recovery key store, Google’s Trusted Vault service. The cloud authenticator includes a mechanism that allows Chrome to facilitate the recovery flow where the key cannot be decrypted on the client device, however this mechanism is not used. Instead, Chrome recovers the SDS in an accessible form. One possible explanation is needing to standardize the device join and recovery process across platforms. Unlike desktop environments, Google Password Manager on iOS and Android does not rely on the cloud authenticator and must obtain the master key to decrypt synced passkeys. As a result, Chrome appears to follow the same recovery model, even though the cloud authenticator could enable a more isolated approach. Although Google removed this secret from Chrome’s logging output following our report, the SDS is still sent to the client and remains accessible in Chrome’s process memory. If the attacker forces the victim to re-register with the cloud authenticator and knows the pattern to look for, they can extract the SDS directly from memory. The Golden Pass-ta-key attack allows full account takeover through the following steps: The attacker forces Chrome to trigger a fresh onboarding using the same mechanisms as the Silver Pass-ta-key attack The attacker monitors the system for the recreation or modification of the passkey_enclave_state Once the file is recreated/modified, the attacker dumps Chrome’s process memory and extracts the SDS, which is temporarily present in plaintext The attacker reads the WebauthnCredentialSpecifics records from Chrome’s sync database (Stage Zero: Reconnaissance) Using the extracted SDS, the attacker decrypts the encrypted fields in each record and recovers the corresponding passkey private keys The attacker uses the recovered private keys to sign the relying party’s challenge and successfully authenticates as the victim Figure 7 shows how an attacker would use the SDS to decrypt passkeys and forge a valid authentication response. Figure 7. Flow of the Golden Pass-ta-key attack. Video 3 shows how an attacker uses the stolen SDS to log in to a high-value account (in this case, a crypto exchange). Video 3. How an attacker uses the stolen SDS to log in to a high-value account. The Golden Pass-ta-key attack has a significantly broader impact. Beyond the reusable access from the attacker’s environment, the SDS allows the attacker to decrypt all existing passkeys as well as any future passkeys created for the account. While the Silver attack is mitigated by unregistering or re-enrolling the device, the Golden attack provides strong persistence. Even if a compromise is detected, remediation is limited. In Google’s current implementation, there is no way to rotate or revoke the SDS, meaning all current and future synced passkeys remain protected by the same master key. Mitigations Enforce Strict User Verification (UV) Validation Relying parties should require userVerification = required and validate the UV flag in all authentication responses. Failure to enforce this check can reduce authentication to a single factor. Figure 8 below shows the authenticator data layout. Figure 8. Authenticator data layout. Source: W3C, Web Authentication. Validate Device Key Registration and Attestation Credential managers should verify the origin and attestation of newly registered device keys, including UV and identity keys. Accepting arbitrary keys without validation allows unauthorized key registration and bypass of user verification requirements. Harden Recovery and Device Re-Registration Flows Credential manager recovery PIN prompts are typically associated with onboarding or account recovery, not routine passkey authentication. Unexpected or repeated prompts during normal passkey usage may indicate re-triggering of onboarding or recovery, potentially due to phishing attempts or local manipulation of passkey state. These flows are security-sensitive because recovery operations can re-establish device trust and restore access to synced credentials. In the scenarios from our research, triggering recovery enabled registration of new verification keys or exposure of key material used to decrypt synced passkeys. Monitoring agents should detect and restrict unnecessary re-triggering of onboarding and recovery flows, especially after deletion or modification of local passkey state files. Additional verification should be required before re-establishing device trust or recovering synced credentials. Prevent Exposure of Sensitive Key Material on the Client Sensitive material such as the master key should not be exposed to the client, including through memory or logs. Instead, credential managers should use designs where cryptographic operations are performed on behalf of the client, without transferring the underlying key material to the client environment. Restrict Access to Local Passkey Data Access to passkey-related storage, such as Chrome’s sync database and local state files (e.g., passkey_enclave_state), should be limited to the browser process and protected through platform access controls. This reduces the ability to enumerate credentials, manipulate onboarding state or access device-bound key material from a compromised endpoint. Improve Detection of Abnormal Passkey Usage WebAuthn defines a signature counter (signCount) mechanism intended to help relying parties detect cloned or unexpectedly reused credentials. In traditional authenticators, the counter increases with each authentication operation and can provide a signal of abnormal credential usage. In synchronized passkey systems, authentication assertions commonly contain a constant signCount value. As a result, relying parties and credential providers have limited visibility into unauthorized use of synced credentials, including scenarios where passkeys are extracted or reused from unexpected environments. Google noted that globally consistent signature counters are difficult to implement in synchronized passkey systems that operate across multiple devices and platforms, particularly when assertions originate from independent clients. Credential managers that centrally coordinate authentication operations should consider implementing coordinated signature counter mechanisms that account for synchronization and multi-device consistency challenges. Such mechanisms can improve visibility and detection of unexpected credential usage or passkey reuse across environments. Conclusion Passkeys represent a meaningful step forward in authentication security. By eliminating shared secrets, they reduce entire classes of attacks that have historically led to widespread account compromise. This changes the economics of credential theft and forces attackers to adopt new techniques. The attacks presented in this research do not break the underlying cryptography. Instead, they exploit gaps between design assumptions and real-world implementations. These gaps include: Trust placed in client devices Inconsistencies in relying party validation Weaknesses in onboarding and recovery flows When combined with malware on the endpoint, these gaps enable account takeover scenarios that bypass the guarantees passkeys are expected to provide. A central takeaway is that endpoint compromise remains a critical part of the threat model. When authentication decisions rely on signals from the user’s device, an attacker with access to that device can manipulate those signals in ways that are difficult to detect. Hardware-backed keys, secure enclaves and cloud isolation significantly raise the bar, but they do not fully eliminate this risk. Passkey deployments should be treated as one layer in a broader security strategy. Relying parties must enforce strict validation, including proper handling of the user verification signal. Platform providers should continue hardening onboarding and recovery flows, and organizations should invest in protections against malware and memory access on endpoints. As adoption continues to grow, so will attacker interest in this space. Understanding these emerging attack paths is essential to ensuring passwordless authentication delivers its intended security benefits in real-world conditions. The resulting blob is stored as wrapped_identity_private_key in the passkey_enclave_state file, making it available for future use on the same physical TPM.

blocks.html_en: The cloud authenticator returns a valid assertion regardless of whether the request was signed using the identity key or the UV key. The difference comes down to a single bit in the authenticator data, the User Verified (UV) flag.

blocks.html_en: To carry out this attack, the first objective is to invalidate the existing UV key associated with the target device. From the previous attack, we learned how an attacker can use unprivileged malware to sign attacker-controlled requests with the device identity key and send them to the cloud authenticator. The attacker can leverage this capability to issue a device/forget command on behalf of the victim. A simpler option is to directly delete the victim’s passkey_enclave_state file, as there are no built-in protections that prevent its removal.

sentences.en: Stealing the Master Key: The Golden Pass-Ta-Key Attack

blocks.html_en: In this attack, the attacker effectively gains the cloud authenticator’s superpower, the ability to decrypt synced passkeys. This is particularly impactful because it undermines the intended protection mechanism.

sentences.en: In this attack, the attacker effectively gains the cloud authenticator’s superpower, the ability to decrypt synced passkeys.

This allows them to authenticate as a fully verified user and take over every service where the victim relies on passkeys.

sentences.zh: 这使他们能够作为经过完全验证的用户进行身份验证，并接管受害者依赖密钥的每项服务。

sentences.en: Leaking the SDS
sentences.zh: 泄露 SDS

blocks.html_en: This secret should never be exposed to the client device, even during device loss or account recovery. However, we unexpectedly found the SDS present in Chrome’s logs during registration with the cloud authenticator, simply by opening chrome://device-log/FIDO, as noted in Figure 6.

sentences.en: This secret should never be exposed to the client device, even during device loss or account recovery.
sentences.zh: 即使在设备丢失或帐户恢复期间，也不应将此秘密暴露给客户端设备。

sentences.en: However, we unexpectedly found the SDS present in Chrome’s logs during registration with the cloud authenticator, simply by opening chrome://device-log/FIDO, as noted in Figure 6.
sentences.zh: 然而，在注册云验证器期间，我们意外地发现 Chrome 日志中存在 SDS，只需打开 chrome://device-log/FIDO，如图 6 所示。

sentences.zh: SDS（​​万能密钥）以明文形式暴露在设备日志中。

blocks.html_en: In the current Chrome implementation, every device joining or rejoining an account’s security domain retrieves the SDS from the recovery key store, Google’s Trusted Vault service. The cloud authenticator includes a mechanism that allows Chrome to facilitate the recovery flow where the key cannot be decrypted on the client device, however this mechanism is not used. Instead, Chrome recovers the SDS in an accessible form.

sentences.en: In the current Chrome implementation, every device joining or rejoining an account’s security domain retrieves the SDS from the recovery key store, Google’s Trusted Vault service.
sentences.zh: 在当前的 Chrome 实施中，加入或重新加入帐户安全域的每台设备都会从恢复密钥存储（Google 的 Trusted Vault 服务）检索 SDS。

sentences.en: The cloud authenticator includes a mechanism that allows Chrome to facilitate the recovery flow where the key cannot be decrypted on the client device, however this mechanism is not used.
sentences.zh: 云身份验证器包含一种机制，允许 Chrome 在密钥无法在客户端设备上解密的情况下促进恢复流程，但并未使用此机制。

sentences.en: Instead, Chrome recovers the SDS in an accessible form.
sentences.zh: 相反，Chrome 以可访问的形式恢复 SDS。

blocks.html_en: One possible explanation is needing to standardize the device join and recovery process across platforms. Unlike desktop environments, Google Password Manager on iOS and Android does not rely on the cloud authenticator and must obtain the master key to decrypt synced passkeys. As a result, Chrome appears to follow the same recovery model, even though the cloud authenticator could enable a more isolated approach.

sentences.en: One possible explanation is needing to standardize the device join and recovery process across platforms.
sentences.zh: 一种可能的解释是需要标准化跨平台的设备连接和恢复过程。

sentences.en: Unlike desktop environments, Google Password Manager on iOS and Android does not rely on the cloud authenticator and must obtain the master key to decrypt synced passkeys.
sentences.zh: 与桌面环境不同，iOS 和 Android 上的 Google 密码管理器不依赖于云身份验证器，并且必须获取主密钥才能解密同步密钥。

sentences.en: As a result, Chrome appears to follow the same recovery model, even though the cloud authenticator could enable a more isolated approach.
sentences.zh: 因此，Chrome 似乎遵循相同的恢复模型，尽管云身份验证器可以实现更加隔离的方法。

blocks.html_en: Although Google removed this secret from Chrome’s logging output following our report, the SDS is still sent to the client and remains accessible in Chrome’s process memory. If the attacker forces the victim to re-register with the cloud authenticator and knows the pattern to look for, they can extract the SDS directly from memory.

sentences.en: Although Google removed this secret from Chrome’s logging output following our report, the SDS is still sent to the client and remains accessible in Chrome’s process memory.
sentences.zh: 尽管谷歌在我们的报告之后从 Chrome 的日志输出中删除了这个秘密，但 SDS 仍然会发送到客户端，并且仍然可以在 Chrome 的进程内存中访问。

sentences.en: If the attacker forces the victim to re-register with the cloud authenticator and knows the pattern to look for, they can extract the SDS directly from memory.
sentences.zh: 如果攻击者强迫受害者重新注册云验证器并知道要查找的模式，他们就可以直接从内存中提取 SDS。

sentences.en: The attacker forces Chrome to trigger a fresh onboarding using the same mechanisms as the Silver Pass-ta-key attack

blocks.html_en: • The attacker monitors the system for the recreation or modification of the passkey_enclave_state

sentences.en: The attacker monitors the system for the recreation or modification of the passkey_enclave_state
sentences.zh: 攻击者监视系统以重新创建或修改 passkey_enclave_state

sentences.en: Once the file is recreated/modified, the attacker dumps Chrome’s process memory and extracts the SDS, which is temporarily present in plaintext

sentences.en: The attacker reads the WebauthnCredentialSpecifics records from Chrome’s sync database (Stage Zero: Reconnaissance)

blocks.html_en: • Using the extracted SDS, the attacker decrypts the encrypted fields in each record and recovers the corresponding passkey private keys

sentences.en: Using the extracted SDS, the attacker decrypts the encrypted fields in each record and recovers the corresponding passkey private keys
sentences.zh: 使用提取的 SDS，攻击者解密每条记录中的加密字段并恢复相应的密钥私钥

sentences.en: The attacker uses the recovered private keys to sign the relying party’s challenge and successfully authenticates as the victim
sentences.zh: 攻击者使用恢复的私钥对依赖方的质询进行签名，并成功作为受害者进行身份验证

blocks.html_en: The Golden Pass-ta-key attack has a significantly broader impact. Beyond the reusable access from the attacker’s environment, the SDS allows the attacker to decrypt all existing passkeys as well as any future passkeys created for the account.

sentences.en: The Golden Pass-ta-key attack has a significantly broader impact.
sentences.zh: Golden Pass-ta-key 攻击具有更广泛的影响。

sentences.en: Beyond the reusable access from the attacker’s environment, the SDS allows the attacker to decrypt all existing passkeys as well as any future passkeys created for the account.
sentences.zh: 除了从攻击者环境中进行可重复使用的访问之外，SDS 还允许攻击者解密所有现有的密钥以及为该帐户创建的任何未来的密钥。

blocks.html_en: While the Silver attack is mitigated by unregistering or re-enrolling the device, the Golden attack provides strong persistence. Even if a compromise is detected, remediation is limited. In Google’s current implementation, there is no way to rotate or revoke the SDS, meaning all current and future synced passkeys remain protected by the same master key.

sentences.en: While the Silver attack is mitigated by unregistering or re-enrolling the device, the Golden attack provides strong persistence.
sentences.zh: 虽然白银攻击可以通过取消注册或重新注册设备来缓解，但黄金攻击提供了强大的持久性。

sentences.en: Even if a compromise is detected, remediation is limited.
sentences.zh: 即使检测到威胁，补救措施也是有限的。

sentences.en: In Google’s current implementation, there is no way to rotate or revoke the SDS, meaning all current and future synced passkeys remain protected by the same master key.
sentences.zh: 在 Google 当前的实施中，无法轮换或撤销 SDS，这意味着所有当前和未来的同步密钥仍受同一主密钥的保护。

sentences.en: Mitigations

blocks.html_en: Enforce Strict User Verification (UV) Validation

sentences.en: Enforce Strict User Verification (UV) Validation
sentences.zh: 执行严格的用户验证 (UV) 验证

blocks.html_en: Relying parties should require userVerification = required and validate the UV flag in all authentication responses. Failure to enforce this check can reduce authentication to a single factor. Figure 8 below shows the authenticator data layout.

sentences.en: Relying parties should require userVerification = required and validate the UV flag in all authentication responses.
sentences.zh: 依赖方应要求 userVerification = required 并验证所有身份验证响应中的 UV 标志。

sentences.en: Failure to enforce this check can reduce authentication to a single factor.
sentences.zh: 如果不强制执行此检查，可能会将身份验证减少到单一因素。

blocks.html_en: Validate Device Key Registration and Attestation

sentences.en: Validate Device Key Registration and Attestation
sentences.zh: 验证设备密钥注册和认证

blocks.html_en: Credential managers should verify the origin and attestation of newly registered device keys, including UV and identity keys. Accepting arbitrary keys without validation allows unauthorized key registration and bypass of user verification requirements.

sentences.en: Credential managers should verify the origin and attestation of newly registered device keys, including UV and identity keys.
sentences.zh: 凭证管理器应验证新注册的设备密钥的来源和证明，包括 UV 和身份密钥。

sentences.en: Accepting arbitrary keys without validation allows unauthorized key registration and bypass of user verification requirements.
sentences.zh: 未经验证而接受任意密钥会导致未经授权的密钥注册并绕过用户验证要求。

blocks.html_en: Harden Recovery and Device Re-Registration Flows

sentences.en: Harden Recovery and Device Re-Registration Flows
sentences.zh: 强化恢复和设备重新注册流程

blocks.html_en: Credential manager recovery PIN prompts are typically associated with onboarding or account recovery, not routine passkey authentication. Unexpected or repeated prompts during normal passkey usage may indicate re-triggering of onboarding or recovery, potentially due to phishing attempts or local manipulation of passkey state.

sentences.en: Credential manager recovery PIN prompts are typically associated with onboarding or account recovery, not routine passkey authentication.
sentences.zh: 凭据管理器恢复 PIN 提示通常与入职或帐户恢复相关，而不是与常规密钥身份验证相关。

sentences.en: Unexpected or repeated prompts during normal passkey usage may indicate re-triggering of onboarding or recovery, potentially due to phishing attempts or local manipulation of passkey state.
sentences.zh: 在正常使用密钥期间出现意外或重复的提示可能表示重新触发登录或恢复，这可能是由于网络钓鱼尝试或对密钥状态的本地操纵造成的。

blocks.html_en: These flows are security-sensitive because recovery operations can re-establish device trust and restore access to synced credentials. In the scenarios from our research, triggering recovery enabled registration of new verification keys or exposure of key material used to decrypt synced passkeys.

sentences.en: These flows are security-sensitive because recovery operations can re-establish device trust and restore access to synced credentials.
sentences.zh: 这些流是安全敏感的，因为恢复操作可以重新建立设备信任并恢复对同步凭据的访问。

sentences.en: In the scenarios from our research, triggering recovery enabled registration of new verification keys or exposure of key material used to decrypt synced passkeys.
sentences.zh: 在我们研究的场景中，触发恢复可以注册新的验证密钥或暴露用于解密同步密钥的密钥材料。

blocks.html_en: Monitoring agents should detect and restrict unnecessary re-triggering of onboarding and recovery flows, especially after deletion or modification of local passkey state files. Additional verification should be required before re-establishing device trust or recovering synced credentials.

sentences.en: Monitoring agents should detect and restrict unnecessary re-triggering of onboarding and recovery flows, especially after deletion or modification of local passkey state files.
sentences.zh: 监控代理应检测并限制不必要的重新触发登录和恢复流程，尤其是在删除或修改本地密钥状态文件之后。

sentences.en: Additional verification should be required before re-establishing device trust or recovering synced credentials.
sentences.zh: 在重新建立设备信任或恢复同步凭据之前，应需要进行额外的验证。

blocks.html_en: Prevent Exposure of Sensitive Key Material on the Client

sentences.en: Prevent Exposure of Sensitive Key Material on the Client
sentences.zh: 防止敏感关键材料暴露在客户身上

blocks.html_en: Sensitive material such as the master key should not be exposed to the client, including through memory or logs. Instead, credential managers should use designs where cryptographic operations are performed on behalf of the client, without transferring the underlying key material to the client environment.

sentences.en: Sensitive material such as the master key should not be exposed to the client, including through memory or logs.
sentences.zh: 主密钥等敏感材料不应暴露给客户端，包括通过内存或日志。

sentences.en: Instead, credential managers should use designs where cryptographic operations are performed on behalf of the client, without transferring the underlying key material to the client environment.
sentences.zh: 相反，凭证管理器应使用代表客户端执行加密操作的设计，而不将底层密钥材料传输到客户端环境。

blocks.html_en: Restrict Access to Local Passkey Data

sentences.en: Restrict Access to Local Passkey Data
sentences.zh: 限制对本地密钥数据的访问

blocks.html_en: Access to passkey-related storage, such as Chrome’s sync database and local state files (e.g., passkey_enclave_state), should be limited to the browser process and protected through platform access controls. This reduces the ability to enumerate credentials, manipulate onboarding state or access device-bound key material from a compromised endpoint.

sentences.en: Access to passkey-related storage, such as Chrome’s sync database and local state files (e.g., passkey_enclave_state), should be limited to the browser process and protected through platform access controls.
sentences.zh: 对密钥相关存储的访问，例如 Chrome 的同步数据库和本地状态文件（例如 passkey_enclave_state），应仅限于浏览器进程，并通过平台访问控制进行保护。

sentences.en: This reduces the ability to enumerate credentials, manipulate onboarding state or access device-bound key material from a compromised endpoint.
sentences.zh: 这降低了枚举凭证、操纵登录状态或从受感染端点访问设备绑定密钥材料的能力。

blocks.html_en: Improve Detection of Abnormal Passkey Usage

sentences.en: Improve Detection of Abnormal Passkey Usage
sentences.zh: 改进对异常密钥使用的检测

blocks.html_en: WebAuthn defines a signature counter (signCount) mechanism intended to help relying parties detect cloned or unexpectedly reused credentials. In traditional authenticators, the counter increases with each authentication operation and can provide a signal of abnormal credential usage.

sentences.en: WebAuthn defines a signature counter (signCount) mechanism intended to help relying parties detect cloned or unexpectedly reused credentials.
sentences.zh: WebAuthn 定义了签名计数器 (signCount) 机制，旨在帮助依赖方检测克隆或意外重用的凭据。

sentences.en: In traditional authenticators, the counter increases with each authentication operation and can provide a signal of abnormal credential usage.
sentences.zh: 在传统的身份验证器中，计数器随着每次身份验证操作而增加，并且可以提供异常凭证使用的信号。

blocks.html_en: In synchronized passkey systems, authentication assertions commonly contain a constant signCount value. As a result, relying parties and credential providers have limited visibility into unauthorized use of synced credentials, including scenarios where passkeys are extracted or reused from unexpected environments.

sentences.en: In synchronized passkey systems, authentication assertions commonly contain a constant signCount value.
sentences.zh: 在同步密钥系统中，身份验证断言通常包含一个常量的signCount值。

sentences.en: As a result, relying parties and credential providers have limited visibility into unauthorized use of synced credentials, including scenarios where passkeys are extracted or reused from unexpected environments.
sentences.zh: 因此，依赖方和凭证提供商对同步凭证的未经授权使用的可见性有限，包括从意外环境中提取或重复使用密钥的情况。

blocks.html_en: Google noted that globally consistent signature counters are difficult to implement in synchronized passkey systems that operate across multiple devices and platforms, particularly when assertions originate from independent clients.

sentences.en: Google noted that globally consistent signature counters are difficult to implement in synchronized passkey systems that operate across multiple devices and platforms, particularly when assertions originate from independent clients.
sentences.zh: 谷歌指出，在跨多个设备和平台运行的同步密钥系统中很难实现全局一致的签名计数器，特别是当断言源自独立客户端时。

blocks.html_en: Credential managers that centrally coordinate authentication operations should consider implementing coordinated signature counter mechanisms that account for synchronization and multi-device consistency challenges. Such mechanisms can improve visibility and detection of unexpected credential usage or passkey reuse across environments.

sentences.en: Credential managers that centrally coordinate authentication operations should consider implementing coordinated signature counter mechanisms that account for synchronization and multi-device consistency challenges.
sentences.zh: 集中协调身份验证操作的凭证管理器应考虑实施协调的签名计数器机制，以解决同步和多设备一致性挑战。

sentences.en: Such mechanisms can improve visibility and detection of unexpected credential usage or passkey reuse across environments.
sentences.zh: 此类机制可以提高跨环境中意外凭证使用或密钥重用的可见性和检测。

blocks.html_en: Conclusion

sentences.en: Conclusion
sentences.zh: 结论

blocks.html_en: Passkeys represent a meaningful step forward in authentication security. By eliminating shared secrets, they reduce entire classes of attacks that have historically led to widespread account compromise. This changes the economics of credential theft and forces attackers to adopt new techniques.

sentences.en: Passkeys represent a meaningful step forward in authentication security.
sentences.zh: 密钥代表身份验证安全性向前迈出了有意义的一步。

sentences.en: By eliminating shared secrets, they reduce entire classes of attacks that have historically led to widespread account compromise.
sentences.zh: 通过消除共享秘密，它们减少了历史上导致广泛帐户泄露的各类攻击。

sentences.en: This changes the economics of credential theft and forces attackers to adopt new techniques.
sentences.zh: 这改变了凭证盗窃的经济原理，并迫使攻击者采用新技术。

blocks.html_en: The attacks presented in this research do not break the underlying cryptography. Instead, they exploit gaps between design assumptions and real-world implementations. These gaps include:

sentences.en: The attacks presented in this research do not break the underlying cryptography.
sentences.zh: 本研究中提出的攻击不会破坏底层密码学。

sentences.en: Instead, they exploit gaps between design assumptions and real-world implementations.
sentences.zh: 相反，他们利用了设计假设和现实世界实现之间的差距。

sentences.en: These gaps include:
sentences.zh: 这些差距包括：

blocks.html_en: • Trust placed in client devices

sentences.en: Trust placed in client devices
sentences.zh: 对客户端设备的信任

blocks.html_en: • Inconsistencies in relying party validation

sentences.en: Inconsistencies in relying party validation
sentences.zh: 依赖方验证不一致

blocks.html_en: • Weaknesses in onboarding and recovery flows

sentences.en: Weaknesses in onboarding and recovery flows
sentences.zh: 入职和恢复流程的弱点

blocks.html_en: When combined with malware on the endpoint, these gaps enable account takeover scenarios that bypass the guarantees passkeys are expected to provide.

sentences.en: When combined with malware on the endpoint, these gaps enable account takeover scenarios that bypass the guarantees passkeys are expected to provide.
sentences.zh: 当与端点上的恶意软件结合使用时，这些漏洞会导致帐户接管场景绕过密钥预期提供的保证。

blocks.html_en: A central takeaway is that endpoint compromise remains a critical part of the threat model. When authentication decisions rely on signals from the user’s device, an attacker with access to that device can manipulate those signals in ways that are difficult to detect. Hardware-backed keys, secure enclaves and cloud isolation significantly raise the bar, but they do not fully eliminate this risk.

sentences.en: A central takeaway is that endpoint compromise remains a critical part of the threat model.
sentences.zh: 一个核心要点是，端点妥协仍然是威胁模型的关键部分。

sentences.en: When authentication decisions rely on signals from the user’s device, an attacker with access to that device can manipulate those signals in ways that are difficult to detect.
sentences.zh: 当身份验证决策依赖于来自用户设备的信号时，有权访问该设备的攻击者可以以难以检测的方式操纵这些信号。

sentences.en: Hardware-backed keys, secure enclaves and cloud isolation significantly raise the bar, but they do not fully eliminate this risk.
sentences.zh: 硬件支持的密钥、安全飞地和云隔离显着提高了标准，但它们并不能完全消除这种风险。

blocks.html_en: Passkey deployments should be treated as one layer in a broader security strategy. Relying parties must enforce strict validation, including proper handling of the user verification signal. Platform providers should continue hardening onboarding and recovery flows, and organizations should invest in protections against malware and memory access on endpoints.

sentences.en: Passkey deployments should be treated as one layer in a broader security strategy.
sentences.zh: 密钥部署应被视为更广泛的安全策略中的一层。

sentences.en: Relying parties must enforce strict validation, including proper handling of the user verification signal.
sentences.zh: 依赖方必须执行严格的验证，包括正确处理用户验证信号。

sentences.en: Platform providers should continue hardening onboarding and recovery flows, and organizations should invest in protections against malware and memory access on endpoints.
sentences.zh: 平台提供商应继续强化加入和恢复流程，组织应投资于针对端点上的恶意软件和内存访问的保护。

blocks.html_en: As adoption continues to grow, so will attacker interest in this space. Understanding these emerging attack paths is essential to ensuring passwordless authentication delivers its intended security benefits in real-world conditions.

sentences.en: As adoption continues to grow, so will attacker interest in this space.

content_html_zh:
执行摘要

本文分析了针对无密码身份验证的新攻击类别，重点关注 Google 的同步密钥生态系统和桌面客户端使用的云身份验证器。 这些攻击展示了受感染端点上的恶意软件如何滥用登录、恢复和设备信任工作流程来接管受密码保护的帐户。 我们展示了攻击者如何在没有用户交互的情况下进行身份验证、绕过用户验证要求并提取所有同步的密钥私钥。

经过数十年的数据泄露和数十亿美元的损失后，定义密码和共享秘密时代的攻击媒介终于开始消失。 万能钥匙用公钥加密技术取代了密码和传统的多重身份验证 (MFA)，从而减少了多年来主导威胁格局的各类攻击。

由于没有可供窃取、重复使用或网络钓鱼的共享秘密，攻击者的许多最可靠的工具正在变得过时。 这对凭证盗窃市场造成了重大破坏。

然而，攻击者依然坚持。 它们不断发展，防御者必须为新一代的攻击做好准备。 随着密钥被广泛采用并扩展到数十亿个帐户，防御者必须为新的攻击面做好准备，我们在研究中披露了其中一些攻击面。

本文是我们从安全角度探讨密钥采用情况系列文章的第 3 部分。 如果您还没有阅读前面的部分，我们建议您从这里开始：

第 1 部分：隐形钥匙的艺术 – Passkey 全球突破

第 2 部分：Google 身份验证器：无密码身份验证的隐藏机制

Palo Alto Networks 通过以下产品和服务更好地保护客户免受这种新的攻击媒介的侵害：

  • Cortex 云身份安全
  • Idira 威胁检测和响应
  • Idira 端点权限管理器
  • Idira 权限访问管理

如果您认为自己可能已受到威胁或有紧急事项，请联系 Unit 42 事件响应团队。

搭建舞台

谷歌的同步密钥实施因其规模以及如何以两种关键方式创建更高的私钥保护标准而特别具有指导意义：

  • 私钥在云飞地隔离环境中生成和使用
  • 硬件支持、客户端设备绑定的密钥控制对基于云的加密操作的访问，证明用户存在​​于受信任的设备上

本文基于本系列之前文章的第 1 部分和第 2 部分的架构分析。 我们现在从如何构建和部署密钥转向攻击者如何滥用它们。

我们提出了三种新颖的攻击，可以接管受密码保护的帐户。 每次攻击都挑战密钥身份验证安全性的不同核心假设。 当客户端使用密钥进行身份验证时，预计会出现以下情况：

  • 用户在设备上明确同意以验证用户的存在
  • 对于 MFA，用户还必须解锁设备以验证生物识别（即您是谁）或基于知识的（即您知道的东西）身份验证因素
  • 密钥私钥无法共享或复制

Google 文档反映了这些核心假设，将密钥登录过程描述为密码的安全替代方案（如图 1 所示）。

挑战这些期望的是一类我们昵称为“密钥传递”的攻击。 这个有趣的、分层的名字融合了“passkey”这个词和“pass the key”这个短语，并轻轻点头了一盘意大利面的概念，说明了这个密钥的实现是多么的复杂。

这些攻击在实践中都暴露了不同的弱点：

  • Pass-ta-key 攻击：攻击者使用受害者设备上运行的恶意软件接管受 Google 同步密钥保护的帐户，无需权限升级、设备解锁或用户交互
  • Silver Pass-ta-key 攻击：攻击者欺骗 Google Cloud Authenticator，让其相信受害者已使用生物识别技术解锁了设备，从而导致在身份验证期间不使用受害者设备的情况下完全接管帐户
  • Golden Pass-ta-key 攻击：攻击者可以以允许在凭证黑市上共享或出售的形式提取所有同步的密钥

这些攻击展示了恶意软件如何利用同步密钥，即使提供商添加了硬件支持的保护来保护云身份验证器中的凭证。

免责声明：这项研究涉及负责任和道德的安全分析。 我们负责任地披露了所有提出的漏洞。 云身份验证器模型由跨多个浏览器和平台的各种密钥提供商使用。 不过，这项工作重点关注 Windows 上 Chrome 中的 Google 密码管理器，特别是配备可信平台模块 (TPM) 的设备。 所有提出的攻击都依赖于在初始阶段受害者设备上已经存在的恶意软件。

零级侦察

在尝试任何攻击之前，攻击者需要了解受害者帐户中如何使用密钥。 在受感染的端点上，这种可见性很容易获得。

作为同步过程的一部分，Chrome 在本地存储同步的密钥数据。 在 Windows 上，Chrome 将此数据保留为原始编码的 WebauthnCredentialSpecifics 记录，这些记录表示同步数据库中的同步 WebAuthn 凭据：

%LocalAppData%\Google\Chrome\User Data\<配置文件>\Sync Data\LevelDB

访问这些记录不需要提升权限。 这些记录允许攻击者枚举受害者使用密钥的位置，以及相关的用户名、凭证标识符和加密的私钥。

在识别出受害者使用密钥的服务后，攻击者可以尝试以受害者身份进行身份验证。

攻击者面临的主要挑战是绕过私钥的保护，私钥用于签署身份验证质询。 该私钥由主密钥保护。 虽然该主密钥的加密版本存储在每个客户端设备上，但只有云身份验证器可以对其进行解密。

尽管有这种安全性，但该架构仍然容易受到攻击。 以下部分详细介绍了攻击者可用于利用系统机制、以受害者身份进行身份验证以及破坏受密钥保护的帐户的方法。

设备身份冒充：传递密钥攻击

我们的第一个攻击是最直接的方法，它涉及通过模仿 Google 密码管理器和 Chrome 在合法身份验证期间的行为来接管受密码保护的帐户。 在正常流程中，Chrome 会向云验证器发送请求，并使用设备的硬件支持密钥进行签名。

与需要用户交互和设备解锁的合法用户流不同，此攻击展示了恶意软件如何在未经用户同意、生物识别、设备解锁或提升权限的情况下悄悄获取所需签名。

为了理解这一点，我们重点关注 Chrome 的设备身份密钥，它代表云身份验证器的客户端设备所有权。 如前所述（第 2 部分：使用同步密钥和设备密钥签名登录），生成所需的断言涉及使用设备的硬件支持密钥之一对发送到云身份验证器的数据进行签名。 这是身份密钥或用户验证密钥（UV 密钥）。

尽管两个密钥都是硬件绑定的，但它们的访问方式不同。 对于身份密钥，Chrome 创建了条件，允许其在以用户身份运行时请求签名，而无需提升权限，也不会触发设备解锁保护。

在 Windows 上，Chrome 调用 NcryptCreatePersistedKey 函数而不分配密钥名称，从而使 TPM 支持的密钥成为临时密钥并阻止其持久保存到磁盘。 Chrome 不是将私钥存储在 TPM 中，而是调用 NcryptExportKey 将密钥导出为 NCRYPT_OPAQUE_KEY_BLOB，这指示 TPM 使用 TPM 驻留密钥加密私钥。 生成的 blob 作为wrapped_identity_private_key 存储在 passkey_enclave_state 文件中，以便将来在同一物理 TPM 上使用。

恶意软件可以从磁盘或 Chrome 内存中提取此wrapped_identity_private_key。 然后，它可以使用标准 Windows 加密 API：下一代 (CNG) API（NCryptOpenStorageProvider、NCryptImportKey、NCryptSignHash）调用加密操作，无需提升权限，模仿 Chrome 自己的操作。

确定恶意软件可以生成所需的签名后，我们现在详细介绍完整的密钥传递攻击流程（如图 2 所示）。 此流程允许在受害者设备上使用非特权恶意软件的远程攻击者以受害者身份进行身份验证。

攻击流程由以下阶段组成：

  1. 收集受害者的同步密钥记录（第零阶段：侦察）后，攻击者选择目标帐户并启动密钥登录
  2. 依赖方以新的身份验证质询进行响应
  3. 攻击者发起与 Google Cloud Authenticator 的 WebSocket 握手
  4. 使用该握手的哈希值，攻击者与受害者的 TPM 进行交互，并使用提取的身份密钥对握手哈希值以及断言请求进行签名
  5. 攻击者向云认证器发送断言请求，包括身份密钥签名
  6. 从云验证器的角度来看，该请求似乎是发出有效请求的受信任设备，因此它会生成有效的断言响应
  7. 然后将该断言转发给依赖方，完成身份验证并使攻击者完全控制受害者的帐户

视频 1 演示了该攻击在实践中的展开情况。 （我们模糊了依赖方的名称以避免点名。）

视频1. 成功的密钥传递攻击示例。

当视频开始时，屏幕在攻击者的终端和受害者的桌面之间分割。 视频首先显示攻击者建立命令和控制 (C2) 侦听器，被动等待受害者连接。

在受害者的计算机上，木马以标准用户身份执行，无需提升权限。 一旦激活，它会收集受害者的加密同步密钥，并将其发送回攻击者的 C2 服务器。 这提供了受害者可用密钥的可见性。

攻击者选择一个目标，例如受密钥保护的消息应用程序帐户，导航到该应用程序并选择使用密钥登录。 然后，依赖方以新的身份验证质询进行响应。

接下来，攻击者发起与 Google Cloud Authenticator 的通信。 完成握手后，攻击者触发木马使用设备的身份密钥对所需数据进行签名。 具体来说，它使用握手的哈希值与序列化断言请求的哈希值相结合。

然后，攻击者将此签名附加到发送到云身份验证器的请求中。 云验证器返回请求的断言。 攻击者将此有效断言转发给依赖方并以受害者身份成功登录。

UV 标志：当 MFA 取决于单个位时

当依赖方不严格要求用户验证时，密码传递攻击是有效的。 许多依赖方将 WebAuthn 的 userVerification 参数配置为首选参数，而不是支持不同设备和用户体验所需的参数，这使得他们容易受到这种攻击。

当依赖方明确要求用户验证时，人们会期望云身份验证器拒绝未使用由 PIN 或生物识别验证控制的密钥签名的请求。 令人惊讶的是，事实并非如此。

无论请求是使用身份密钥还是 UV 密钥签名，云验证器都会返回有效的断言。 差异归结为身份验证器数据中的一个位，即用户已验证 (UV) 标志。

当使用 UV 密钥对断言进行签名时，该标志设置为 1。 当使用身份密钥对其进行签名时，该标志保持为 0。

虽然 Pass-ta-key 攻击会产生与依赖方公钥匹配的加密有效断言，但我们的测试表明，当需要用户验证时，攻击通常会失败，因为 UV 标志仍未设置。 例如，当尝试攻击受密码保护的 GitHub 帐户时，攻击者会收到一条错误消息，如图 3 所示。

尽管在需要用户验证时身份验证通常会被拒绝，但这种行为并不总是在依赖方之间一致执行。 在我们的测试中，我们确定了接受身份验证的依赖方，因为他们没有正确验证 UV 标志。 尽管没有用户验证，这使得攻击得以成功。

缺乏验证有效地将身份验证过程简化为单一因素。 通过仅泄露设备身份密钥，攻击者就能够成功进行身份验证并接管帐户，即使需要 MFA。

待定攻击者：Silver Pass-Ta-Key 攻击

当帐户受到更严格的身份验证要求（例如金融或联邦身份系统）保护时，攻击者还必须绕过用户验证。 乍一看，这似乎是一个重大挑战。

云验证器需要使用 UV 密钥签名的消息来设置 UV 标志。 客户端交互控制对此密钥的访问，因为操作系统通过与设备解锁相同的机制来验证用户。 在不升级到系统权限或对受害设备进行物理访问的情况下，攻击者没有明显的途径来获取此类访问权限。

攻击者可以通过以下机制绕过此挑战：

  • 攻击者不是绕过对 UV 密钥的访问，而是使云验证器中注册的现有密钥无效，并在其控制下注册新生成的密钥
  • 一旦攻击者控制的密钥被注册，任何用它签名的消息都会被云验证器接受，就像用户已成功执行设备解锁一样

这种方法具有重要意义。 它允许攻击者在无需人工交互的情况下对所有受害者的帐户进行完全自动化的身份验证，即使在强制执行用户验证的情况下也是如此。 此外，攻击者在身份验证期间不再需要实时访问受害者的设备。

与之前的攻击不同的是，每次身份验证都需要受害者设备上存在活动恶意软件，而银牌攻击提供了可重用的访问权限。 这使得攻击者可以从自己的环境访问受害者受密码保护的帐户，而无需受害者的设备在线或处于活动状态。 最终，这使得可以接管与受害者相关的所有密钥的帐户，而无需提升权限。

使已有的用户验证密钥失效

要执行此攻击，第一个目标是使与目标设备关联的现有 UV 密钥失效。 从之前的攻击中，我们了解到攻击者如何使用非特权恶意软件使用设备身份密钥对攻击者控制的请求进行签名，并将其发送到云身份验证器。 攻击者可以利用此功能代表受害者发出设备/忘记命令。 一个更简单的选择是直接删除受害者的 passkey_enclave_state 文件，因为没有内置保护措施可以阻止其删除。

无论采用哪种方法，下次用户尝试使用密钥时，Chrome 都会被迫重新登录设备。 发生这种情况的原因可能是 Chrome 无法再访问设备密钥，或者是因为云身份验证器不再将设备识别为注册设备。

利用入职流程

在 Windows 上，只有在同一设备上第二次使用密钥后才能完成设备登录。 首次使用期间，Chrome 会开始在后台使用云身份验证器，同时提示用户输入 Google 密码管理器 (GPM) 恢复 PIN 码。

如果 Chrome 此时创建 UV 密钥，它还会触发 Windows Hello 提示，要求用户使用生物识别或 PIN 再次进行身份验证。 由于这两个步骤都可能涉及 PIN，因此在同一流程中连续呈现它们可能会造成混乱并导致用户错误。 为了避免这种情况，Chrome 推迟了 UV 键的创建。

相反，设备最初注册为 uv_key_pending 状态。 在第一次交互期间，GPM 恢复 PIN 满足用户验证，并且仅在下次使用密钥时（当不再需要附加提示时）创建并注册实际的 UV 密钥。

在迫使受害者进入重新注册状态后，攻击者可以利用 uv_key_pending 条件。 在自己的环境中，攻击者生成非对称密钥对。 然后，他们向云验证器发送 device/add_uv_key 命令，提供攻击者控制的公钥作为 UV 密钥。

云验证器不会验证新注册的 UV 密钥的证明来验证它们是否源自安全硬件。 因此，攻击者控制的密钥与合法设备身份密钥一起存储：

窃取万能钥匙：Golden Pass-Ta-Key 攻击

在这次攻击中，攻击者有效地获得了云验证器的超能力，即解密同步密钥的能力。 这尤其具有影响力，因为它破坏了预期的保护机制。

密钥的私钥使用称为安全域秘密 (SDS) 的对称主密钥进行保护。 该主密钥无法直接访问，它作为加密的wrapped_secret 存储在设备上。 只有云身份验证器可以在其隔离环境中使用其设备特定密钥 (wrapping_key) 解密此wrapped_secret，如图 5 所示。

此设计旨在即使客户端设备受到威胁也能保护同步密钥。 正如谷歌在回应我们的一份漏洞报告时指出的那样：

“（云）enclave 身份验证器的主要功能是使窃取密钥私人数据变得困难，如果这些数据在本地可用，那么这些数据将成为恶意软件的明显目标。”

该模型的安全性最终取决于32字节SDS的保护。 如果攻击者能够获取 SDS，他们就能有效地解密该帐户的所有同步密钥。 这使他们能够作为经过完全验证的用户进行身份验证，并接管受害者依赖密钥的每项服务。

泄露 SDS

即使在设备丢失或帐户恢复期间，也不应将此秘密暴露给客户端设备。 然而，在注册云验证器期间，我们意外地发现 Chrome 日志中存在 SDS，只需打开 chrome://device-log/FIDO，如图 6 所示。

在当前的 Chrome 实施中，加入或重新加入帐户安全域的每台设备都会从恢复密钥存储（Google 的 Trusted Vault 服务）检索 SDS。 云身份验证器包含一种机制，允许 Chrome 在密钥无法在客户端设备上解密的情况下促进恢复流程，但并未使用此机制。 相反，Chrome 以可访问的形式恢复 SDS。

一种可能的解释是需要标准化跨平台的设备连接和恢复过程。 与桌面环境不同，iOS 和 Android 上的 Google 密码管理器不依赖于云身份验证器，并且必须获取主密钥才能解密同步密钥。 因此，Chrome 似乎遵循相同的恢复模型，尽管云身份验证器可以实现更加隔离的方法。

尽管谷歌在我们的报告之后从 Chrome 的日志输出中删除了这个秘密，但 SDS 仍然会发送到客户端，并且仍然可以在 Chrome 的进程内存中访问。 如果攻击者强迫受害者重新注册云验证器并知道要查找的模式，他们就可以直接从内存中提取 SDS。

Golden Pass-ta-key 攻击允许通过以下步骤完全接管帐户：

  1. 攻击者使用与 Silver Pass-ta-key 攻击相同的机制强制 Chrome 触发新的登录
  2. 攻击者监视系统以重新创建或修改 passkey_enclave_state
  3. 一旦文件被重新创建/修改，攻击者就会转储 Chrome 的进程内存并提取暂时以明文形式存在的 SDS
  4. 攻击者从 Chrome 的同步数据库中读取 WebauthnCredentialSpecifics 记录（第零阶段：侦察）
  5. 使用提取的 SDS，攻击者解密每条记录中的加密字段并恢复相应的密钥私钥
  6. 攻击者使用恢复的私钥对依赖方的质询进行签名，并成功作为受害者进行身份验证

Golden Pass-ta-key 攻击具有更广泛的影响。 除了从攻击者环境中进行可重复使用的访问之外，SDS 还允许攻击者解密所有现有的密钥以及为该帐户创建的任何未来的密钥。

虽然白银攻击可以通过取消注册或重新注册设备来缓解，但黄金攻击提供了强大的持久性。 即使检测到威胁，补救措施也是有限的。 在 Google 当前的实施中，无法轮换或撤销 SDS，这意味着所有当前和未来的同步密钥仍受同一主密钥的保护。

缓解措施

执行严格的用户验证 (UV) 验证

依赖方应要求 userVerification = required 并验证所有身份验证响应中的 UV 标志。 如果不强制执行此检查，可能会将身份验证减少到单一因素。 下面的图 8 显示了验证器数据布局。

验证设备密钥注册和认证

凭证管理器应验证新注册的设备密钥的来源和证明，包括 UV 和身份密钥。 未经验证而接受任意密钥会导致未经授权的密钥注册并绕过用户验证要求。

强化恢复和设备重新注册流程

凭据管理器恢复 PIN 提示通常与入职或帐户恢复相关，而不是与常规密钥身份验证相关。 在正常使用密钥期间出现意外或重复的提示可能表示重新触发登录或恢复，这可能是由于网络钓鱼尝试或对密钥状态的本地操纵造成的。

这些流是安全敏感的，因为恢复操作可以重新建立设备信任并恢复对同步凭据的访问。 在我们研究的场景中，触发恢复可以注册新的验证密钥或暴露用于解密同步密钥的密钥材料。

监控代理应检测并限制不必要的重新触发登录和恢复流程，尤其是在删除或修改本地密钥状态文件之后。 在重新建立设备信任或恢复同步凭据之前，应需要进行额外的验证。

防止敏感关键材料暴露在客户身上

主密钥等敏感材料不应暴露给客户端，包括通过内存或日志。 相反，凭证管理器应使用代表客户端执行加密操作的设计，而不将底层密钥材料传输到客户端环境。

限制对本地密钥数据的访问

对密钥相关存储的访问，例如 Chrome 的同步数据库和本地状态文件（例如 passkey_enclave_state），应仅限于浏览器进程，并通过平台访问控制进行保护。 这降低了枚举凭证、操纵登录状态或从受感染端点访问设备绑定密钥材料的能力。

改进对异常密钥使用的检测

WebAuthn 定义了签名计数器 (signCount) 机制，旨在帮助依赖方检测克隆或意外重用的凭据。 在传统的身份验证器中，计数器随着每次身份验证操作而增加，并且可以提供异常凭证使用的信号。

在同步密钥系统中，身份验证断言通常包含一个常量的signCount值。 因此，依赖方和凭证提供商对同步凭证的未经授权使用的可见性有限，包括从意外环境中提取或重复使用密钥的情况。

谷歌指出，在跨多个设备和平台运行的同步密钥系统中很难实现全局一致的签名计数器，特别是当断言源自独立客户端时。

集中协调身份验证操作的凭证管理器应考虑实施协调的签名计数器机制，以解决同步和多设备一致性挑战。 此类机制可以提高跨环境中意外凭证使用或密钥重用的可见性和检测。

结论

密钥代表身份验证安全性向前迈出了有意义的一步。 通过消除共享秘密，它们减少了历史上导致广泛帐户泄露的各类攻击。 这改变了凭证盗窃的经济原理，并迫使攻击者采用新技术。

本研究中提出的攻击不会破坏底层密码学。 相反，他们利用了设计假设和现实世界实现之间的差距。 这些差距包括：

  • 对客户端设备的信任
  • 依赖方验证不一致
  • 入职和恢复流程的弱点

当与端点上的恶意软件结合使用时，这些漏洞会导致帐户接管场景绕过密钥预期提供的保证。

一个核心要点是，端点妥协仍然是威胁模型的关键部分。 当身份验证决策依赖于来自用户设备的信号时，有权访问该设备的攻击者可以以难以检测的方式操纵这些信号。 硬件支持的密钥、安全飞地和云隔离显着提高了标准，但它们并不能完全消除这种风险。

密钥部署应被视为更广泛的安全策略中的一层。 依赖方必须执行严格的验证，包括正确处理用户验证信号。 平台提供商应继续强化加入和恢复流程，组织应投资于针对端点上的恶意软件和内存访问的保护。

随着采用率的不断增长，攻击者对这一领域的兴趣也会随之增加。 了解这些新兴的攻击路径对于确保无密码身份验证在现实条件下发挥其预期的安全优势至关重要。
